items.title: Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy

dossiers.title: Hate Plus
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The central interaction is searching archived ship records and reading conversations with companion AIs to reconstruct a generations-long political collapse, not combat or conventional puzzles.
AIs *Mute and *Hyun-ae comment on recovered logs; players particularly praise the nuanced characters, themes of social coercion and emotionally affecting dialogue.
Three game days of log recovery are separated by a real-time waiting requirement of roughly 12 hours, which some players appreciate for reflection but others consider unnecessary forced downtime.

Most reading choices and conversations have limited impact on the predetermined main narrative; route differences center on which AI companion accompanies the protagonist and certain ending variations.
New groups of archived records and cross-linked character information gradually reveal the ship's history; progression is primarily narrative rather than skill or equipment upgrades.
Players accustomed to traditional adventure games may dislike the scarcity of puzzles and lack of strongly branching decision consequences.
The story's darker political tragedy and the cross-referencing of historical names reward careful reading but also make long sequences of text potentially demanding.

A Russian-language community guide describes a fan translation that replaces Korean while retaining English, achievements and save compatibility; this is a user-generated workaround and not evidence of official Russian localization.

conflicts.statement: The tragic AI-character writing is often praised while some players object that companion choices rarely avert predetermined story outcomes.

dossiers.title: Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy

game_identity.work_title: Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy

dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: One mouse-controlled hammer supplies all the movement for climbing a continuous mountain of improvised obstacles, with swings, pushes and careful hooks as the basic techniques.
A single missed catch can erase hours of climbing progress, making the game exceptionally punishing and emotionally frustrating to many players.
Views on the hammer physics are sharply split: some report unpredictable or unresponsive motions while others describe learning a precise, nonlinear system through practice.
No persistent skills, upgrades, checkpoints or levels soften the repeated climb; progress comes mainly from learning the mountain and improving player dexterity.
Repeatedly revisiting the same early obstacles after major falls builds muscle memory, but can become demoralizing or boring rather than rewarding.
The philosophical narrator, music and intentionally provocative humor are considered meaningful context by some players and pretentious or distracting by others.
A single ascending route and a succession of recognizable difficult zones replace quests, character progression or exploration of independent areas.
Players who persist often report relief or satisfaction when mastering a previously impossible movement, while negative responses emphasize that one slip can negate that feeling.

Some late-2025 players still discuss inconsistent hammer traction and jumps, but available comments do not establish a reproducible current technical defect distinct from the intentional control physics.

conflicts.statement: The deliberate loss of progress is exhilarating mastery for some, but makes the mouse-driven climbing feel unfair or pointless for others.

dossiers.title: PAYDAY™ The Heist
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 10 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Four-player first-person heists require completing drills, carrying objectives and surviving escalating police assault waves under fire, with little emphasis on extended stealth.
Player accounts strongly favor coordinated human teams, with complementary cover and revive actions carrying more weight than solo shooting.
AI teammates can support firefights but generally will not restart drills or complete heist objectives, so solo players shoulder the work and find hard missions less forgiving.
Players earn levels, class upgrades and equipment unlocks through repeated robberies, but some find early leveling restrictive and endgame weapon choice distorted by the meta.
Higher difficulty heists punish weak team positioning and expose a substantial gap between ordinary and Overkill 145+ play.
The compact pool of repeatable maps permits mastery and changing team strategies, while some players tire of the most popular bank map and routine drill defense.
Russian-speaking players report long online loading, lobby friction, peer-host disconnections and game bugs; these historical accounts do not establish the current service state.
The criminals-versus-police atmosphere and highly mobile firefights provide an action identity, while some players criticize dated animation and limited scripted activity diversity.
Discrete large heist levels and varied objectives are replayed to build equipment and skill; this is a mission-based co-op shooter, not an open-world robbery campaign.
Discussion participants disagree about playing with bots: some complete many heists alone but others find the coordination and difficulty far better with friends.

conflicts.statement: The co-op tactical appeal and memorable heists are praised, but bot limitations and dependence on effective public lobbies can undermine solo play.
